text:
⚖️ 800 Posts: The Names, the Inventories, and the Unfinished Reckoning

Hungary’s 1944 seizure files name the Jewish owners whose possessions were taken from their homes. They record paintings, books, furniture and silver alongside addresses, measurements, crate markings and instructions for transfer. More than eighty years later, that paperwork can reconnect a surviving object with the household from which it was taken—and help establish whether it was ever returned.

Across 800 posts, the Holocaust Art Recovery Initiative has pursued those connections. Working principally through Reels 143–145 of the Hungarian microfilm collection at the Zekelman Holocaust Center, HARI has examined the state’s own record of dispossession alongside family histories, museum catalogues, auction records and surviving objects. This final installment brings that work together: the people identified, the transfers documented, the possible matches awaiting examination, and the evidence still needed to resolve their histories.

For Clara Garbon-Radnoti, the connection between an inventory and a family was painfully personal. While examining the microfilm, she recognized her widowed aunt’s name and address. The possessions included a rolling pin, four kitchen chairs and a kitchen table. Her aunt and the aunt’s young daughter did not survive deportation. Clara sent the record to the cousin who had survived. Behind an administrative entry was a home she knew—and people whose absence no inventory could measure.

The same attention belongs to every household in these files, whether its possessions included an Old Master painting, a scientific library or the furnishings of an ordinary room. A surviving inscription, an unusual measurement or a confiscation number can provide a lead across decades of missing history. Following it requires three distinct inquiries: Is this the same object? Was it returned to its owner or successors? What does its subsequent ownership history establish? Evidence of restitution and lawful sale matters as much as evidence of seizure. A persuasive match begins that investigation; it does not settle the claim.

The legal developments of 2026 make completing these histories especially consequential. The April HEAR Act amendments changed the framework for covered Holocaust-era property claims, and the July remand of 26 Herzog claims reopened a path to further proceedings. Neither development supplies the missing ownership evidence. That work still depends on accessible files, careful examination and the participation of heirs and communities.

Eight hundred posts cannot exhaust the archive or resolve every claim. They can identify where the next inquiry should begin. A named owner, a documented taking and a plausible surviving object create a concrete reason to investigate. The institutions holding the objects and the remaining records have an essential part in what happens next.

📜 A SURVIVOR’S WORK MADE THE RECORD ACCESSIBLE

This undertaking rests on work that preceded the first HARI post. Professor Randolph L. Braham donated the microfilm collection to the Zekelman Holocaust Center in 1992. Hungarian Holocaust survivor Clara Garbon-Radnoti devoted a decade to its English finding aid and translated key material from Reels 143–145. Her work gave researchers a practical way into thousands of difficult Hungarian records. Librarian Feiga Weiss connected Clara with HARI () founder Jonathan H. Schwartz. Their collaboration was the subject of a January 29, 2019 Detroit News story, years before these online posts. The work began with a survivor reading the records of the society that had persecuted her and helping others understand what they contained.

The Zekelman Holocaust Center and the World Jewish Restitution Organization announced the online archive in February 2025. The Claims Conference–WJRO Looted Art & Cultural Property Initiative allocated funding for digitization and translation, with support credited to the Foundation “Remembrance, Responsibility and Future” and the German Federal Ministry of Finance.

HARI built on that preservation and translation work. The series brought individual pages into public discussion, connected bureaucratic entries to biographies, compared wartime descriptions with museum and auction records, and identified the further evidence needed to confirm or reject proposed matches. The underlying documents remain the authority; every interpretation must remain open to correction.

🏛️ THE MUSEUM DIRECTOR AND THE CONFISCATION ADMINISTRATION

Dénes Csánky simultaneously directed Budapest’s Museum of Fine Arts and served as government commissioner responsible for registering and safeguarding sequestered Jewish artworks. His commissioner’s office operated from the museum. The files show how cultural expertise became part of a state apparatus that identified, assessed, selected, inventoried, transported, and stored Jewish-owned property.

The correspondence connects national museums with finance authorities, police, municipalities, banks, libraries, teachers, dealers, restorers, and local museum personnel. The series followed instructions, requests for assistance, proposed allocations, inventories, transport arrangements, and receipts. Each records a different stage; together, they reveal how an administrative program reached into individual homes.

The language often emphasized preservation and “safekeeping.” Meanwhile, owners were being excluded from public life, forced from their homes, confined in ghettos, deported, and murdered. Protecting the physical condition of an object could coexist with destroying its owner’s control over it. A museum’s custody of a painting therefore has to be investigated alongside the circumstances in which that custody began.

👤 CULTURAL PROFESSIONALS MADE PARTICULAR CHOICES

The records repeatedly identify people whose other achievements are celebrated in cultural histories. HARI examined Elemér Kőszeghy’s role inside the Herzog Palace; Béla Darnay’s handling of material through the Balaton Museum; and András Soós’s involvement in Jewish reader lists and the subsequent selection and packing of books and artworks in Nagyvárad, now Oradea.

In Baja, painter and museum official Ferenc Miskolczy requested Jewish labor servicemen to collect confiscated objects. His own paintings also appear in the inventories of local Jewish collectors. The request documents his intention to use forced labor; it does not establish that the men were supplied. In Nagykanizsa, painter and art dealer László Bujdoss sought the authority and equipment needed to act as a local delegate, including a typewriter from confiscated property. In Békéscsaba, József Mokos’s work selecting Jewish-owned art was connected explicitly to enlarging the museum.

Other files expose proposals for the property’s use. Carpet specialist Béla Kiss reported submitting a list of 43 Jewish collectors and urged state possession of their carpets. Lajos Ujváry proposed using seized books to reward pupils. The Göcsej Association sought books, pictures, furnishings, and a house without payment to establish cultural institutions. Museum director Lajos Kiss, in Nyíregyháza, proposed selling rejected paintings to artists who could paint over them. These proposals reveal how readily dispossessed people’s belongings could be treated as resources for somebody else’s work.

Csánky’s own interventions extended beyond his Budapest office. The Losonc correspondence records his travel and his deputy’s demands for assistance. The Sepsiszentgyörgy files include directions to trace Jewish-owned artworks with police help. The series also examined his response to Emil Stein’s request for relief from anti-Jewish restrictions. These histories require attention to the acts recorded in each file, including the difference between a proposed action and a completed one.

🗺️ FROM THE CAPITAL TO REGIONAL DEPOTS

The geographical reach was extensive. In Pécs, Jewish-owned objects were gathered in the synagogue, and the files refer to a 146-page inventory. In Kassa, now Košice, correspondence connected the clearing of Jewish homes to museum custody. The Szeged dossier spans 101 microfilm slides across Reels 143 and 144. Baja supplies successive household inventories, allowing named families and addresses to be followed through the local operation.

The repeated appearance of Mihály Munkácsy’s name across inventories became a separate line of inquiry, including a church official’s report of a signed painting and instructions for taking it under seal through Szombathely. Each entry must be tested against its own owner, subject, medium, measurements, and custody record; the artist’s name alone cannot identify which surviving painting the file describes.

The series also examined records from Beregszász/Berehove, Munkács/Mukachevo, Ungvár/Uzhhorod, Nagyvárad/Oradea, Szabadka/Subotica, Losonc/Lučenec, Sepsiszentgyörgy/Sfântu Gheorghe, Nagykanizsa, Keszthely, Sopron, Győr, Kaposvár, Szolnok, and other towns. These records now cross national borders and languages. Historical place names, changing institutional names, and later transfers all affect where evidence can be found.

In Szombathely, architect and commissioner’s delegate János Tóth described five overcrowded depots on September 26, 1944. Furniture reached the ceilings. Porcelain lay in crates by the thousand. 843 carpets had been packed for an intended transfer to Budapest that was postponed. He reported “an unbelievable quantity of gold and silver” and anticipated museum-worthy objects among the silver before inspecting it. The report captures the scale of accumulated Jewish property and the officials’ concern with its potential institutional value. It does not establish the final destination of everything described. (Reel 145, slides 145–147.)

🖼️ HERZOG AND THE COLLECTIONS AROUND IT

The Herzog investigations became a major strand of the series. The files from Andrássy út 93, the Budafok cellars, and related locations connect the Herzog family with the histories of Kiss, Sváb, Weiss, Kornfeld, and Mauthner property. Those connections require object-by-object analysis: a shared address, crate, family relationship, or storage location does not make ownership interchangeable.

HARI examined paintings in these files and their later identifications and attributions, including works associated with El Greco, Giovanni Santi, Isenbrandt, Giampetrino, Goya, Renoir, Courbet, Alvaro Pirez, and others. The investigations included Santi’s Misericordia Domini, now catalogued in Budapest as The Man of Sorrows, inventory 51.799; the Isenbrandt triptych panels 9047/a–c; Giampetrino’s Christ Carrying the Cross, 58.2; and the histories surrounding El Greco’s Saint Andrew, 51.800, and the workshop Holy Family with Saint Anne, 50.755. Some cases concern previously published ownership histories; others concern proposed identifications or unresolved transfers. They cannot all be counted as new discoveries or completed recoveries.

The scope extended well beyond paintings. Herzog research addressed an Egyptian mummy mask, inventory 9818, for which published scholarship identifies Herzog provenance; a Late Bronze Age sword candidate at the Hungarian National Museum; jewelry, gems, and coins recorded in 259 numbered entries; and a wartime receipt for seven numbered furniture pieces associated with the Royal Hungarian Opera House. Other inquiries concerned an Egyptian necklace, sculpture, a terracotta or stucco Madonna, and further household and decorative objects.

These investigations ask more than where a celebrated painting hangs. They ask how a family collection was divided, how objects were relabeled or redistributed, which pieces were returned, and how later legal and institutional records account for the rest.

🔎 THE EVIDENCE THAT CAN CONNECT AN OBJECT TO ITS OWNER

The comparisons bring together attribution, subject, medium, dimensions, owner, address, condition, inscriptions, frame labels, crate marks, and receipts. Each supplies a different test. An inscription naming a former owner, a wartime photograph, and a close dimensional correspondence carry different kinds of evidentiary weight; they should be explained on their own terms.

An owner’s name on the reverse. A Glatz Transylvanian Village examined in the series bears an inscription connecting Mrs. Sándor Sváb with Andrássy út 93. Such marks can preserve a relationship omitted from a later catalogue. High-resolution photographs of the back of a painting—its verso—along with its frame, stretcher, labels, and stamps can therefore be as consequential as its frontal image.

A numbered label inside a book. Item 41 in Sándor Fleischl’s wartime library inventory was Wilhelm Müseler’s Geist und Antlitz der Gotik. A copy offered in 2026 bore both Fleischl’s ownership mark and the Government Commissioner’s label “Fleischl 41.” Author, title, binding, owner, and wartime item number converge on the surviving book. Its subsequent history, including whether it was returned after the war, remains to be reconstructed. (Reel 144, slides 432–441; Item 41 on slide 437.)

The Topers: a painting visible in the seizure’s publicity. HARI compared a May 20, 1944 Herzog crate entry for Goya’s Ivók, 101 × 79.5 cm, with The Topers at the North Carolina Museum of Art, inventory 56.13.1. Fundación Goya en Aragón publishes a size of 101 × 80 cm. The connection goes beyond measurements: Konstantin Akinsha’s 2011 study identifies the painting in the Herzog collection and reproduces a Magyar Futár photograph of Hungarian secret policemen with it. He also records its later reclassification as “in the style of Goya.” Wartime presence and the subsequent ownership chain are separate questions; the route to the Babcock Foundation and the museum still needs a documented account.

Other paintings in wartime photographs. HARI examined proposed identifications involving El Greco’s workshop, Alonso Cano, and Károly Brocky in Magyar Futár imagery. These photographs were produced in the setting of antisemitic seizure publicity. Read critically, they can help establish which works were present, alongside the inventories and receipts.

Brocky and the Kornfeld-marked crate. The 1944 record describes Woman in Black, oil on canvas, 76 × 47 cm, and damage to red drapery. The Hungarian National Gallery’s 50.572 matches the artist, subject, medium, and dimensions. The condition note supplies an additional test: whether conservation records and examination of the painting reveal a corresponding history.

Gerrit Dou and the Surányi inventory. A June 1944 entry records an Alabárdos, or halberdier, in Dr. Miklós Surányi’s collection: oil on panel, 66 × 51 cm. HARI compared it with the Museum of Fine Arts’ Dou, inventory 62.10, with the same dimensions and a closely corresponding subject. The Surányi research also examined the inventory’s Brueghel-follower Wedding against a Peasant Wedding catalogued as workshop of Marten van Cleve, inventory 7560.

Pieter Jansz. Quast and Mihály Vadász. The wartime Musical Company entry measures 49.2 × 36.5 cm. Budapest’s Merry Company Making Music, inventory 71.20, is catalogued at 49 × 36.5 cm. That close correspondence supplies a precise question for the museum’s acquisition and ownership records.

Alvaro Pirez and the “Blessing Christ.” A 1944 protocol’s early-fifteenth-century Italian panel, in tempera, has a painted surface of 91 × 59 cm. Budapest’s The Risen Christ, inventory 51.801, has a painted surface of 90.5 × 59.6 cm. The comparison demonstrates why research must distinguish the painted surface from the dimensions of an entire support or frame.

The Csetényi collection. Research extended from Rachel Ruysch and Jan van Os still lifes to a Sébastien Bourdon portrait candidate, a Triumphal March, and an eighteenth-century pastel compared with Portrait of Julia Czindery, inventory 9840. Principal inventories, secondary “selejt” lists, delivery records, and frame labels offer different routes into the same collection. A lesser administrative classification did not erase an owner’s rights. Postwar recovery and later dispersal make return and sale records essential to each object’s history.

Attribution changes can fragment a search. A work described under one artist’s name in 1944 may now be catalogued under a workshop, follower, or different painter. Titles change too. These revisions are not evidence of concealment, but they explain why a single artist-name search can miss a relevant object. Researchers must compare the composition, support, measurements, markings, and condition across successive descriptions.

🌍 BUDAPEST RECORDS, INTERNATIONAL QUESTIONS

The search extended into museums and markets far beyond Hungary. At the National Museum of Women in the Arts in Washington, D.C., a Ruysch floral still life, inventory 1986.282, measures 107.95 × 83.82 cm, compared with 107 × 82 cm in the Csetényi record. Another Csetényi inventory entry, a French seventeenth-century male portrait measuring 105 × 88 cm, was compared with Bourdon’s Portrait of a Man at the Art Institute of Chicago, published at 104.2 × 88.1 cm. In Canada, the Agnes Etherington Art Centre’s Koninck Panoramic River Landscape with Hunters, 55-005, measures 105 × 135 cm, against a wartime description of 105 × 136 cm. Each comparison narrows a research question; its differences and ownership gaps remain part of the test.

The Caravaggio Saint John the Baptist investigation followed a recurring 99 cm width from a 135 × 99 cm wartime entry into later auction comparisons. Width alone cannot uniquely identify a painting. Composition, support, alterations, old photographs, and the pre-auction ownership chain must be examined together.

Other inquiries reached Harvard’s Fogg Museum through a Tiepolo comparison; London through Rubens-related material; Madrid through a Machuca inquiry; New York through Schiele-related research; and Russian repositories through displaced books. Auction research followed works attributed to Hans Canon, Eugène Carrière, Auguste Lepère, and others through Vienna, Paris, Budapest, and additional markets.

The questions also extend to Lipót Fejér’s scientific library in Fukuoka. Kyushu University identifies 786 volumes as Fejér’s former books and records their purchase in 1965. Establishing which volumes, if any, passed through the documented wartime seizure requires the acquisition records and examination of the books themselves. A named collection abroad provides a place to investigate; it does not establish an unbroken confiscation-to-institution chain.

🏺 FURNITURE, ANTIQUITIES, TEXTILES, AND ORDINARY HOUSEHOLDS

The Hatvany-Deutsch files recorded paintings, textiles, furniture, books, arms, and military subjects. HARI compared a Renaissance-style chest from the Hatvan Castle inventory with Museum of Applied Arts inventory 61.332.1. The Lánchíd utca file documented distinct routes for books and objects sent to the Museum of Fine Arts and the military museum. Those separate lists and dates have to be preserved when reconstructing the household’s losses.

The series also followed the Kaszab, Weiser, Munther, Doroghy, Szilárd, Politzer, Littmann, Strauss, Dobay, and Madarassy-Beck records. Investigations included Thorma and Maticska paintings; Rippl-Rónai pastels; Iványi Grünwald’s Old Violinist; Zichy’s Scottish Torch Dance; a Napoleon death-mask candidate; a bronze Abduction of the Sabine Women plaque; a polychrome Saint Paul; and a small Madonna on copper examined against a Scarsellino attribution. Additional studies addressed works by Mednyánszky, Vastagh, Csók, Ligeti, and Markó.

Bank-safe openings, apartment inventories, and museum intake sheets brought these different media into the same documentary field. A ceramic, a carpet, a musical instrument, an archaeological object, and a room of furnishings could all carry a traceable ownership history. Their importance does not depend on appearing in an Old Master gallery.

The Jenő Lázár archaeological collection made the stakes especially clear: a museum could itself become the object of an inventory while its Jewish founder was in Auschwitz. The subsequent claim that the material was company property requires scrutiny alongside the circumstances of its creation and seizure. Institutional descriptions can obscure the person whose work assembled a collection.

📚 THE LIBRARIES: BOOKS, OWNERS, AND INTELLECTUAL LIVES

HARI’s library investigations followed individual books, entire private collections, manuscripts, scholarly working materials, synagogue libraries, and communal archives. They examined the Kornfeld, Fleischl, Hatvany-Deutsch, Gáspár, Fejér, and Kadelburg collections, as well as Jewish and Zionist libraries in Sopron and bulk book records elsewhere.

The Hatvany-Deutsch shelves placed art-historical monographs alongside The Children’s Book of Art. The inventory covered Rembrandt studies, a Vigée Le Brun monograph, and older books on subjects extending well beyond painting. The children’s volume supplies a different scale of cultural loss: the books through which a household could introduce another generation to art.

The record of Endre Gáspár’s library included a two-volume English Ulysses. He survived and produced the novel’s first complete Hungarian translation, published in 1947. The distinct Bernát Gáspár case concerned a library and literary manuscripts, including an English translation of Madách’s The Tragedy of Man. Bookplates, manuscript packets, crate counts, and library receipts can preserve an intellectual life that a generic entry for “books” conceals.

The Kornfeld library research followed successive removals and the later dispersal of books, including material associated with Russian repositories. The Sopron files showed Jewish writing and Jewish subjects singled out in the cataloguing process. Győr’s postwar records raised questions about tens of thousands of books and competing proposals for their allocation. A proposal to assign a library to an institution must be distinguished from proof that the assignment occurred.

🎨 ARTISTS AND OWNERS WHO CANNOT BE REDUCED TO INVENTORY ENTRIES

Lajos Kunffy wrote from the Tab ghetto about albums, photographs, and approximately 100 drawings that should go to the county museum if he died. After obtaining an exemption, he asserted his right to recover control of the material. The sequence preserves an artist’s intentions: a conditional bequest, a demand for return, and the continuing work for which he needed his archive. Those intentions must remain distinct from later accounts of wartime losses.

József Pécsi, the photographer, asked for advance notice so that he could be present when officials came to select and remove his antique furniture. András Novák, the applied-arts teacher and designer, was ordered to gather the artistic objects in his apartment into a lockable room, prepare their inventory himself, and preserve them pending official sealing. The letter threatened criminal liability for failing to comply. He survived to continue his design career; the letter records a moment when the state compelled him to prepare his own domestic surroundings for its control.

Móric Barát’s name appears beside 32 works in a Nagyvárad collection-center inventory. He was murdered at Auschwitz. HARI also examined works by Tibor Ernő, murdered at Dachau, and Paula Porter, murdered in 1944, whose Balaton appears in a sealed-apartment inventory from that year. These records can help reconstruct artistic legacies even where the present location of the works remains unknown.

The Klára Geréb investigation connected an artist and a Jewish family with the Dömötör Palace in Subotica, the building from which she was deported and which later became the municipal museum. It also examined a separate wartime ambition to enlarge the museum with seized Jewish art. The building’s later cultural use should make the earlier family history more visible.

Róza Grünwald’s inventory preserved a collection including Sándor Bihari’s Venetian Kitchen, which HARI compared with a later auction work. Károly Dénes’s sword bequest required a different distinction: his testamentary decision, made under persecution, could not simply be equated with later officials’ proposals or an applicant’s wish to buy seventeen swords. The owners’ choices, the coercion surrounding them, and subsequent dealings all belong in the record.

text:
This Anthropic IPO allocation strategy was suboptimal and myopic. I heard from many long-only firms that received zero shares and they were VERY annoyed.

You want to spread the allocation as much as possible across long-term oriented firms that invest on multi-year time frames. 

Giving them a starter position makes them much more likely to buy more in the aftermarket, rather than ticking them off.

Allocating more shares to hedge funds or rewarding friendly early VC firms that are more likely flip and already have massive exposure is not the best approach. 

Anthropic needs to think about building allies in the next chapter, not the past.

quoted_text:
They should have allocated more shares to long-term oriented long-only investors. That's basic IPO strategy stuff.

WSJ: "Some investors question how the company and its bankers doled out the $81 billion worth of shares in the IPO. More than half went to investors who already had stakes in the company, including Altimeter Capital, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Menlo Ventures, according to people familiar with the matter, an unusually high portion reflecting Anthropic executives’ desire to reward early backers.

Some of those early backers were venture-capital firms, which were prevented from selling their pre-existing stakes. Those firms don’t typically get big allotments in IPO shares, which they would be free to sell immediately to lock in gains."
